title: Mindfulness Seminar 5
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness by being present with one's feelings, body sensations, and thoughts, rather than getting caught up in analysis or intellectualization. This involves taking responsibility for one's own practice, staying with difficult experiences, and trusting one's intuition to guide the way. By doing so, one can develop greater awareness, clarity, and freedom from mental activity, allowing for a more authentic and peaceful experience of life.

So a few clarifying words about the second foundation of mindfulness.
I took a sort of big run at Buddhist psychology in a way last week that maybe was not necessarily that helpful, a little confusing maybe.

The idea of mindfulness of feelings is more simply just to be more sensitive and accurately aware of feelings in all of their manifestations, including this sort of sense of positive and negative, but also including what we consider conventional feelings, with this particular interest in what is pleasant and what is unpleasant.

I think I might have been presenting it as sort of a complicated technical sort of feat, like prying the lid open of your mind and seeing something under there you did not see before, which it could be, but it actually could be quite simply just noticing, just noticing more accurately, more carefully what you are feeling.
What am I actually feeling?

Just like with awareness of body and breath, they are all complete, they are so analogous that what is interesting about mindfulness practice is we all go into it thinking, we go into it thinking that it is so obvious.
I know I have a body, I know where the body is.
I know I have breath, I know that I am breathing.
We all know these things in some way.

But as we engage in these practices over time, we realize there are different levels or different ways of knowing, and there are plenty of ways in which I have no clue most of the time where my body is.

I have been noticing lately with awareness of body that what I have been surprised by is you would think that when the body is really in motion, like when you are exercising, you would think that would be a time when you would be aware of your body, right?
You are using the body; the body is like front and center and foremost.

What I have been noticing is when I have been riding my bike or jogging on my little machine at the Y, once in a while I remember to notice my body, and I feel this enormous complicated, sensory sort of thing, my whole body that I was not actually aware of before I tuned into it.
I have been surprised by that that even when the body is active, it is possibly completely unaware that you have a body, even while you are exercising the body and moving the body.
What I notice is that when I am aware of the body, it is a lot more fun, it is a lot more pleasant to move it.
It is the same thing with the feelings.
We think we know what we are feeling, but it might be that we are just dimly aware of an idea of what we are feeling, or it might be that we are only aware of the most acute and the loudest feelings.
